title: Curve Mirror
description: A roadside convex mirror on an orange pole, standing over an old house at a level crossing in Kyoto. Drag to turn it on its bracket and the glass sweeps everything the photograph never showed: the street behind you, the road below, the sky over your head, and, turned far enough, the house and the crossing you are looking at, seen from where the mirror stands. At one angle it catches the sun.
intent: The Japanese curve mirror (カーブミラー, https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/カーブミラー), the convex road mirror at every blind corner, composited into a real photograph as a physical object, and reflecting correctly. Reality pieces research (factory/reality/techniques.md, idea 7, Curve mirror). The photograph is measured: MoGe-2 metric point map, the true vertical from the poles' vanishing point, the sun from the house's shading. The mirror is a traced sphere cap (800 mm, 1.6 m radius of curvature) reflecting one panorama centred on it: the photo's own pixels re-projected from the mirror's position in front of the lens, a Poly Haven street HDRI turned to the photo's sun and given the photo's sky behind it. Frame, shell, bracket and pole are lit by that panorama and the sun, cast their shadow on the house through the point map, and the glass carries dust and a smudge that scatter the sun. Developed through the lab's summer film. ?aim=yaw,pitch holds the aim (degrees), ?aim=sun holds the sun in the glass.

sources.author: PJH (@dokae)
sources.note: Ukyo, Kyoto (Ricoh GR II): a low-angle fumikiri crossbuck and lamps over an old tiled house. Resampled to 2464x1632 (photo.webp). Point map, normals and field of view: MoGe-2 ViT-S normal (Microsoft, MIT, https://huggingface.co/Ruicheng/moge-2-vits-normal-onnx) via tools/depth/normals.py; sky matte tools/depth/segment.py sky. Baked by tools/depth/bakes/curve-mirror (vp.py vertical, bake.py panorama, distances, SH9, shadow aux).

sources.author: Greg Zaal
sources.note: The hemisphere behind the lens: turned so its sun's azimuth is the photo's, exposed to the photo's sunlit walls, its pale sky replaced by a fit of the photo's own sky by elevation, its sun disc removed (the sun is drawn analytically).
